rubric.why: Identifies alkanes as the simplest family of hydrocarbons.
rubric.description: States what family alkanes belong to.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying alkanes as the simplest hydrocarbons.

rubric.why: Specifies that both types of bonds are single bonds.
rubric.description: States which bonds occur in alkanes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that alkanes contain only carbon–carbon and carbon–hydrogen single bonds.

modelAnswer: Alkanes are the simplest family of hydrocarbons with only carbon – carbon and carbon – hydrogen single bond.

rubric.why: Identifies cracking as a process involving hydrocarbons with higher molecular masses.
rubric.description: Identifies the process and the hydrocarbons being broken up.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that cracking is a process involving higher-molecular-mass hydrocarbons.

rubric.why: States that the larger hydrocarbons are broken into smaller, more-demanded hydrocarbons.
rubric.description: States the result and purpose of cracking.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that cracking breaks hydrocarbons into smaller hydrocarbons that are more in demand.

modelAnswer: Cracking is the name of a process in which hydrocarbons with higher molecular masses (which are lesser in demand) are broken up into smaller hydrocarbons which are more in demand.

rubric.why: Identifies replacement of hydrogen in alkanes as the defining change.
rubric.description: States what is replaced and where.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that hydrogen in alkanes is replaced.

rubric.why: Identifies an atom or group of atoms, such as a halogen, as the replacement.
rubric.description: States what replaces the hydrogen and names the reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the replacing atom or group (for example, a halogen) and calling it a substitution reaction.

modelAnswer: The reactions which involve the replacement of hydrogen of alkanes by an atom or a group of atoms like halogen are called substitution reactions.

rubric.why: States that hydrogen is added in an addition reaction.
rubric.description: Identifies the substance added and the change.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that hydrogen is added.

rubric.why: Specifies that the hydrogen is added to an unsaturated compound.
rubric.description: Identifies the type of compound involved.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that hydrogen is added to an unsaturated compound.

modelAnswer: An addition reaction occurs when hydrogen (H₂) is added to an unsaturated compound.

rubric.why: Gives the close electronegativity values or explains that bonding electrons are shared almost equally.
rubric.description: Explains why the bonds in alkanes are nearly non-polar.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that carbon and hydrogen have similar electronegativities (2.6 and 2.1), or that the bond electrons are almost equally shared.

rubric.why: Links the non-polarity of alkane bonds to their unreactivity.
rubric.description: Connects bond polarity to the low reactivity of alkanes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that alkanes are unreactive because their bonds are non-polar.

modelAnswer: The unreactivity of alkanes may be explained on the basis of the non-polarity of the bonds present in them. The electronegativity values of carbon (2.6) and hydrogen (2.1) do not differ appreciably and the bonding electrons between C – H and C – C bonds, are almost equally shared. This fact makes alkanes almost non-polar.

rubric.why: States that alkanes burn in oxygen or air.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that alkanes burn in oxygen or air.

rubric.why: Names the products and the evolution of heat.
rubric.description: States the products of combustion and the heat released.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that carbon dioxide and water form, with heat released.

modelAnswer: Alkanes burn in oxygen or air to form CO₂ and H₂O with the evolution of large amount of heat. The reaction is called combustion.
